overview:
Iran, known for most of its history as Persia, is a large country in Southwest Asia stretching from the Caspian Sea in the north to the Persian Gulf in the south. It borders seven countries, including Iraq, Türkiye, Afghanistan and Pakistan, and covers about 1.65 million km², roughly the size of Alaska. Around 88 million people live there, most in cities such as the capital, Tehran, which sits beneath snow-capped mountains.

Persian, also called Farsi, is the national language, written in a form of the Arabic script, and many Iranians also speak Azerbaijani, Kurdish or other languages. Most people are Shia Muslims. Iran has been an Islamic Republic since a revolution in 1979; a Supreme Leader holds the highest authority, alongside an elected president and parliament.

Iranians are proud heirs of one of the world's oldest civilizations, famous for poetry, gardens, carpets and science. The country holds some of the largest oil and gas reserves on Earth, and its relations with Western countries have been tense for decades.
landAndNature:
Iran is a high, dry land ringed by mountains. The Zagros range runs down the west, and the Alborz rises along the Caspian coast, crowned by Mount Damavand, a dormant volcano about 5,610 meters high, the tallest peak in the Middle East. In the interior lie two great deserts, the Dasht-e Kavir and the Dasht-e Lut, where satellites have measured some of the hottest ground temperatures ever recorded, above 70 degrees Celsius.

The Caspian shore, by contrast, is green and rainy, with rice paddies and tea gardens. Summers are scorching and winters can be snowy, especially in the northwest. Iran is the last home of the Asiatic cheetah, with only a few dozen left, and also shelters Persian leopards, wild sheep, brown bears and flamingos on its salt lakes.
peopleAndCulture:
Persian poetry runs deep in Iranian life; verses by Hafez, Rumi, Ferdowsi and Omar Khayyam are quoted at dinner tables, and families gather on the longest night of the year to read poems and eat pomegranates and watermelon. Nowruz, the new year on the first day of spring, is celebrated for two weeks with a table of symbolic objects, spring cleaning and visits to relatives.

Iranian food features saffron rice with a crispy golden bottom called tahdig, grilled kebabs, herb stews like ghormeh sabzi, and yogurt, fresh herbs and flatbread with every meal. Persian carpets, hand-knotted in intricate patterns, take months or years to make. Wrestling is the traditional national sport, soccer draws huge crowds, and Iran is a world power in weightlifting and volleyball.
history:
Around 550 BC Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, which became the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from Greece to India; its capital, Persepolis, still stands in ruins. Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC, but new Persian dynasties, the Parthians and Sasanians, ruled for centuries more. Arab armies brought Islam in the 600s, and Persian scholars such as Avicenna led the medieval world in medicine, astronomy and mathematics.

The Safavid dynasty made Shia Islam the state religion in the 1500s and built glorious Isfahan. In 1935 the country asked to be called Iran. In 1953 a coup backed by Britain and the United States strengthened the Shah, whose rule ended in the 1979 revolution led by Ayatollah Khomeini. A brutal war with Iraq followed from 1980 to 1988, and disputes over Iran's nuclear program have shaped its relations with the world since.
funFacts: Persian engineers built qanats, underground water tunnels, about 3,000 years ago, and many still carry water to desert towns.
Ancient Iranians built yakhchals, dome-shaped ice houses that kept ice frozen through desert summers without electricity.
Iran produces about 90 percent of the world's saffron, the most expensive spice, picked by hand from crocus flowers.
The Lut Desert holds the record for the hottest land surface ever measured from space, over 70 degrees Celsius.
Backgammon and polo were both played in ancient Persia, and polo may have been invented there.
Windcatchers, tall towers that pull cool breezes into houses, have kept Iranian homes cool for centuries.
